subject: maths

moments.title: The Chevalier de Méré's gambling problem
moments.who: Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat (by letter)
moments.body:
Antoine Gombaud, the Chevalier de Méré, a French nobleman and gambler, poses a problem to Pascal: if a game of chance is interrupted before completion, how should the stakes be divided?

The 'problem of points': two players are betting on a game with multiple rounds. They've played some rounds; one leads. Game stops. Who gets what?

Pascal writes to Fermat in Toulouse. Over a few months of letters, the two work out a complete theory of expected value, conditional probability, and fair division.
moments.takeaway: Probability theory is born from a question about how to settle gambling debts.

moments.title: Huygens publishes the first probability treatise
moments.body:
Christiaan Huygens, having heard about the Pascal-Fermat correspondence, writes 'De Ratiociniis in Ludo Aleae' (On Reasoning in Games of Chance). The first published systematic treatise on probability.

He introduces the concept of expected value and applies it to various dice and card games. The text becomes the standard reference for the next 50 years.
moments.takeaway: Probability becomes a published discipline. Expected value is the central concept.

moments.title: Jacob Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi
moments.who: Jacob Bernoulli, Basel (posthumous publication by nephew Nicolaus)
moments.body:
Jacob Bernoulli works for years on a comprehensive probability text. He proves the LAW OF LARGE NUMBERS: as the number of trials increases, the observed frequency of an outcome converges to its true probability.

He dies in 1705 with the work unfinished. His nephew Nicolaus publishes it in 1713 as Ars Conjectandi (The Art of Conjecturing).

quote.text: It must be confessed that even when we cannot use mathematics to determine the chance of an event, we may approximate the chance by observing how often that event has occurred in past similar circumstances.

moments.takeaway: The law of large numbers connects long-run frequency to probability — the foundation of frequentist statistics.

moments.title: De Moivre's normal distribution
moments.body:
Abraham de Moivre, a French Huguenot refugee in London, works on approximating binomial probabilities for large n. He derives what we now call the normal distribution (the bell curve) as the limit.

He publishes 'The Doctrine of Chances' (1718, expanded 1738), the most comprehensive probability text of its time. He earns a meagre living tutoring rich amateurs and consulting on annuities.
moments.takeaway: The normal distribution appears for the first time, as a limit of binomial trials.

moments.title: Laplace's Théorie Analytique
moments.body:
Laplace publishes a 700-page Théorie Analytique des Probabilités, synthesising and extending all previous work. He proves the Central Limit Theorem (in a special case): the sum of independent random variables tends to a normal distribution.

The book applies probability to astronomy, demography, jurisprudence. It cements probability as a mathematical discipline with broad applications.
moments.takeaway: Probability becomes a respectable mathematical discipline applicable to almost any scientific domain.

now.title: Probability today
now.body:
Probability theory was rigorously axiomatised by Kolmogorov (1933) on measure-theoretic foundations. Modern probability underlies statistics, machine learning, finance, physics (quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics), information theory, and game theory.

Applications: weather forecasting, financial derivatives, search-engine ranking, AI, epidemiological modelling, sports analytics, navigation.
now.open_questions: What's the philosophical status of probability for one-shot events? How do we communicate uncertainty effectively to non-specialists? Why do humans systematically err in probabilistic reasoning? Can quantum probability be embedded in classical probability?

reflection: Probability began as a gambling problem and was developed by some of history's greatest mathematicians as an honour-bound intellectual exercise. The connection between everyday risk and abstract mathematics has produced enormous practical fruit — but also enabled industries (insurance, finance, gambling) that exploit human cognitive limits. How should the abstract success of probability be reconciled with its concrete moral applications?
